q: Ordinary AC ammeters and voltmeters are calibrated to read the:
o: Average values over a whole cycle
x: AC meters show rms values, the steady DC values that would give the same heating; the 220 V of the mains is an rms value. The average over a whole cycle is zero, so it would be useless.

q: A steady DC supply of 10 V and a sinusoidal AC supply produce heat at the same rate in a given resistor. The peak value of the AC voltage is:
x: Equal heating means the rms value of the AC is 10 V, and V₀ = √2 × V(rms) = 10√2 V (about 14 V). Dividing by √2 instead of multiplying gives 5√2 V.

q: A sinusoidal alternating current of peak value 2 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated in the resistor is:
x: P = I(rms)²R = (I₀²/2)R = (4/2) × 10 = 20 W. Using the peak current, I₀²R, gives 40 W.

q: For the 50 Hz mains supply, how many times each second does the current reverse its direction?
x: Each cycle contains two reversals of direction (one in each half-cycle), so 50 cycles per second give 100 reversals per second. 50 counts only the cycles.

q: Two alternating voltages of the same frequency are v₁ = V₀ sin ωt and v₂ = V₀ cos ωt. Which statement is correct?
x: cos ωt = sin(ωt + 90°), so v₂ reaches each value a quarter cycle earlier than v₁: v₂ leads by 90°. For example, v₂ is at its peak at t = 0, when v₁ is still zero.

q: In an AC circuit, the voltage is v = 200 sin(ωt + π/3) V and the current is i = 5 sin(ωt − π/6) A. The phase relation between them is:
o: The current leads the voltage by 90°
The voltage leads the current by 90°
The voltage leads the current by 30°
x: The phase difference is π/3 − (−π/6) = π/3 + π/6 = π/2 = 90°, with the voltage ahead, as in a pure inductor. Subtracting π/6 from π/3 instead (ignoring the minus sign) gives 30°.

q: The reactance of a capacitor to a steady direct current (frequency zero) is:
o: Equal to its reactance at 50 Hz
Infinitely large, so the capacitor blocks steady DC once charged
x: XC = 1/(2πfC), and as f → 0, XC → ∞. A steady current cannot pass through the insulating gap once the capacitor is charged. A zero reactance at DC belongs to an inductor.

q: The reactance of an inductor, XL, and of a capacitor, XC, are each plotted against the frequency f of the supply. Which description is correct?
o: XL is a straight line through the origin; XC falls in inverse proportion to f
XL falls in inverse proportion to f; XC is a straight line through the origin
Both are straight lines through the origin
Both are horizontal lines, independent of frequency
x: XL = 2πfL is directly proportional to f, a straight line through the origin, while XC = 1/(2πfC) is inversely proportional to f, a curve that falls as f rises. Swapping the two is the usual slip.

q: A choke (a coil of large inductance and small resistance) is used instead of a resistor to limit the alternating current in a fluorescent tube circuit, because the choke:
o: Has a very high resistance to AC
Wastes very little energy as heat
Increases the voltage across the tube at all times
x: A choke limits current through its reactance; in an ideal inductor the average power over a cycle is zero, so little energy is lost as heat. A resistor limiting the same current would waste I²R continuously.

q: An inductor of 0.1 H with negligible resistance has a reactance of 31.4 Ω. The frequency of the supply is (π ≈ 3.14):
x: XL = 2πfL, so f = XL/(2πL) = 31.4/(2 × 3.14 × 0.1) = 31.4/0.628 = 50 Hz. Forgetting the 2π gives 314 Hz; forgetting just the 2 gives 100 Hz.

q: A coil connected to a 10 V DC supply draws 2 A. Connected to a 10 V rms AC supply, it draws 1 A rms. The inductive reactance of the coil at the AC frequency is:
x: On DC only resistance acts: R = 10/2 = 5 Ω. On AC the impedance is Z = 10/1 = 10 Ω, and Z² = R² + XL², so XL = √(100 − 25) = √75 = 5√3 Ω (about 8.7 Ω). Taking XL = Z − R gives 5 Ω; taking it as Z gives 10 Ω.

q: A series circuit has R = 60 Ω, XL = 120 Ω and XC = 40 Ω. Its power factor is:
x: Net reactance = 120 − 40 = 80 Ω, so Z = √(60² + 80²) = 100 Ω and the power factor cos φ = R/Z = 60/100 = 0.6. 0.8 is X/Z (sin φ); 0.5 uses XL alone.

q: In a series RLC circuit connected to an AC supply, the rms voltages across the resistor, inductor and capacitor are 30 V, 70 V and 30 V. The rms supply voltage is:
x: VL and VC are 180° apart, so their net is 70 − 30 = 40 V, at 90° to VR: V = √(30² + 40²) = 50 V. Adding all three as numbers gives 130 V; 70 V adds VR to the net reactive voltage.

q: The power factor of a series RLC circuit at resonance is:
x: At resonance XL = XC, so Z = R and the current is in phase with the voltage: φ = 0 and cos φ = 1. A power factor of 0 belongs to a pure inductor or capacitor.

q: A series RLC circuit is connected to an AC supply whose frequency is below the circuit's resonant frequency. Then:
o: XL is greater than XC, and the current leads the supply voltage
XC is greater than XL, and the current lags the supply voltage
XC is greater than XL, and the current leads the supply voltage
XL equals XC, and the current is in phase with the voltage
x: Below resonance f is smaller, so XL = 2πfL is smaller and XC = 1/(2πfC) is larger. The circuit is capacitive overall and the current leads the voltage. Above resonance it is inductive and the current lags.

q: A 0.1 H inductor is to be used with a capacitor in a series circuit that resonates at 50 Hz. The capacitance needed is (take π² ≈ 10):
x: f = 1/(2π√(LC)) gives C = 1/(4π²f²L) = 1/(4 × 10 × 2500 × 0.1) = 1/10 000 F = 100 μF. Check: LC = 10⁻⁵, √(LC) ≈ 3.16 × 10⁻³ s, and 1/(2π × 3.16 × 10⁻³) ≈ 50 Hz. Forgetting to square f leads to a much larger value.

q: In an electromagnetic wave travelling through a vacuum, the oscillating electric and magnetic fields are:
o: Parallel to each other and to the direction of travel
Perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
Perpendicular to each other but along the direction of travel
Parallel to each other and perpendicular to the direction of travel
x: An electromagnetic wave is transverse: E and B oscillate at right angles to each other, and both at right angles to the direction in which the wave moves.

q: The speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum is related to the permeability μ₀ and permittivity ε₀ of free space by:
x: Maxwell's theory gives c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀); with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ this is about 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. 1/(μ₀ε₀) is c², not c.

q: FM radio reception is usually less affected by electrical noise than AM reception because:
o: Noise mainly changes the amplitude of the received wave, and FM does not carry its signal in the amplitude
FM waves travel faster than AM waves
FM uses a lower carrier frequency than AM
Noise cannot reach FM waves, which travel only by reflection from the ionosphere
x: Electrical interference mostly adds random changes of amplitude. In AM the signal is the amplitude, so the noise is heard; in FM the signal is in the frequency, and the receiver can clip off amplitude changes. All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed.

q: In a three-phase supply, the voltage between any one line and the neutral is 220 V. The voltage between any two of the lines is about (√3 ≈ 1.73):
x: The two line voltages are 120° apart, so the p.d. between them is √3 times the phase voltage: 1.73 × 220 ≈ 380 V. Simply adding the two (440 V) ignores the 120° phase difference.

q: In radio broadcasting, the audio signal is carried on a high-frequency carrier wave mainly because:
o: High-frequency waves travel faster than audio-frequency waves
High-frequency waves carry no energy, so they are cheaper to send
Audio-frequency waves would need impractically long aerials and are not radiated efficiently
x: An efficient aerial is comparable in size to the wavelength; a 1 kHz wave has λ = 300 km, so audio cannot be radiated directly. Modulating a high-frequency carrier gives short wavelengths and practical aerials. All electromagnetic waves travel at c.
